points.text: This is an era of managing AIs, rather than working with them.
This new approach to AI is the outcome of the rapid exponential improvement in AI abilities.
That means you can’t understand where we are, and where we might be going, without understanding the increasing capability of AI.
AI remains jagged, capable of some tasks at a high level, while messing up others.
companies are still very early in adopting AI, meaning that, as of yet, remarkably little has changed in most organizations.
the particular details of the Software Factory matter less than the fact that such radical experimentation into how we work is now not only possible, but likely necessary.
AI is good enough to change how organizations operate, and the experimentation is just getting started, even as models continue to improve.
As AI capability crosses thresholds, it unlocks radical new use cases that change people’s views, sometimes overnight, about what AI can do.
as AI continues to improve, more policymakers will become interested in AI governance, creating conflicts with AI companies.

recursive self-improvement, or RSI. This is the idea that AI systems are increasingly being used to build better AI systems, creating a feedback loop that could accelerate the very curves I showed you above.

I don’t think we know anything for certain, but I also think we are past the point when recursive self-improvement is science fiction. Instead, it is an explicit item on the roadmap of every major AI company.
If the loop does close, the exponential curves we’ve been watching would get steeper, with an uncertain endpoint.
We clearly don’t have rules or role models for how AI gets used at work, in schools, or in government.
every organization figuring out a good way to use AI right now is setting a precedent for everyone else.

mappings.explanation: The claim suggests a shift toward managing AI rather than working with it, which contradicts the safetyist emphasis on maintaining direct human control and oversight.
The claim explicitly attributes the new approach to AI to rapid exponential improvement in capabilities, aligning with the scaling hypothesis.
The claim asserts that understanding AI's trajectory requires understanding its increasing capability, which is central to the accelerationist view.

mappings.nodeLabel: Judge AI by Actions, Not Code
mappings.explanation: The claim acknowledges the 'jagged' nature of AI performance, which supports the accelerationist argument for empirical, task-based evaluation.
The claim notes that little has changed in most organizations, contradicting the accelerationist view that AI is already significantly boosting work.
The claim advocates for radical experimentation as a necessity, which aligns with the accelerationist view of permissionless innovation.
The claim asserts that AI is good enough to change operations and that experimentation is underway, supporting the accelerationist view.
The claim describes AI crossing thresholds and changing views, which aligns with the accelerationist perspective on rapid progress.

mappings.nodeLabel: Safety Rules That Protect Big Tech Monopolies
mappings.explanation: The claim anticipates conflicts between policymakers and AI companies, which aligns with the accelerationist concern about regulatory capture.
The claim describes recursive self-improvement as a feedback loop that accelerates progress, a core accelerationist tenet.
The claim asserts that recursive self-improvement is an explicit roadmap item, supporting the accelerationist view of rapid advancement.
The claim acknowledges the potential for steeper exponential curves, which aligns with accelerationist forecasting.
The claim highlights the lack of rules or role models for AI use, which aligns with the safetyist call for governance and control.
The claim emphasizes the importance of setting precedents through current experimentation, aligning with the accelerationist view of decentralized progress.
